title: Office of Inspector General — Independent Oversight
description: U.S. federal Office of Inspector General mission blueprint: one mission with the outcomes it seeks and ways to measure them, five capabilities with their reference requirements, example implementation patterns with their tradeoffs, and discovery question sets for mission results and for intake and case handling. It builds on Common Capabilities for identity, access, data protection, and case management.
jurisdictions: United States — federal Offices of Inspector General

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 404 — Duties and responsibilities of Inspectors General
sources.note: Principal statutory duties of federal Inspectors General.

sources.title: Oversight.gov — Mission of Inspectors General
sources.note: Describes independent oversight, prevention of fraud, waste and abuse, and reporting.

sources.title: Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency — Frequently Asked Questions
sources.note: General description of OIG missions, independence, audits, investigations, and reporting.

sources.title: Oversight.gov — Report Fraud, Waste, Abuse or Retaliation
sources.note: Official routing information for reports of fraud, waste, abuse, or retaliation.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 402 — Establishment and purpose of Offices of Inspector General
sources.note: The purposes of Offices of Inspector General: audits and investigations; economy, efficiency, and effectiveness; preventing and detecting fraud and abuse; and keeping the agency head and Congress fully and currently informed.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 405 — Reports
sources.note: What each semiannual report must include, such as questioned costs, funds put to better use, open recommendations, and investigative statistics, with its deadlines.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 407 — Complaints by employees
sources.note: Receiving employee complaints, keeping a complainant’s identity confidential, and protection from reprisal.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 420 — Information on websites of Offices of Inspectors General
sources.note: Posting audit, inspection, and evaluation reports within 3 days, and a direct link for reporting fraud, waste, and abuse.

sources.title: Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency — Quality Standards for Federal Offices of Inspector General (Silver Book)
sources.note: The overall standards for OIGs, including independence in fact and in appearance, confidentiality, and following the professional standards for audits, investigations, inspections, and evaluations.

sources.title: Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency — Quality Standards for Investigations (July 2025)
sources.note: Standards for investigations in OIGs, replacing the 2011 edition. Among them, investigative information is to be stored securely so it can be retrieved effectively, with personal and other sensitive information protected.

sources.title: Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency — Quality Standards for Inspection and Evaluation (Blue Book)
sources.note: Standards for planning, evidence, documentation, supervision, and reporting in inspections and evaluations.

sources.title: U.S. Government Accountability Office — Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book)
sources.note: The standards for audits of government entities, including audit documentation, supervision, and quality management. The 2024 revision applies to audits beginning on or after December 15, 2025.

sources.title: Public Law 115-414 — Good Accounting Obligation in Government Act (GAO-IG Act)
sources.note: Agencies report, in their annual budget justifications, on public GAO and Inspector General recommendations that remain open.

sources.title: NIST — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.note: A framework for voluntary use in managing the risks of AI systems, built around four functions, govern, map, measure, and manage, and the characteristics of trustworthy AI, such as being valid, accountable, and fair.

elements.title: Office of Inspector General
elements.description: Provide independent and objective oversight to prevent and detect fraud, waste, and abuse; promote economy, efficiency, and effectiveness; and communicate findings and recommendations concerning federal programs and operations.

attributes.tagline: Independent oversight of government programs and operations
principles: The office runs its own systems, administering them and deciding who sees its work, as its independence requires
Each matter is one record from intake to closure, and each engagement one record from plan to its last recommendation
The identity of people who report is kept apart from the allegation from the first contact
Statistics for the semiannual report come from the systems of record, not from spreadsheets
Agency officials send corrective action updates into the office’s tracker through their own access
Analytics and AI suggest, and staff decide

elements.title: Programs and operations run economically, efficiently, and effectively
elements.description: Agency programs and operations make good use of public money and do what they’re meant to do, helped by the office’s audits, inspections, evaluations, and recommendations.

measures.title: Funds recommended for better use
measures.description: The dollar value of recommendations that funds be put to better use, and how much of it management agreed to. Semiannual reports to Congress include these figures.

elements.title: Fraud, waste, and abuse are prevented and detected
elements.description: Wrongdoing in agency programs and operations is deterred, found, and acted on, through audits, investigations, and referrals for prosecution where warranted.

measures.title: Questioned and unsupported costs
measures.description: Costs that audit, inspection, and evaluation reports question, including unsupported costs, and how much of them management disallowed. Semiannual reports to Congress include these figures.

measures.title: Investigative results
measures.description: Investigative reports issued, people referred to the Department of Justice and to state and local prosecutors, and the indictments and criminal informations that followed. Semiannual reports to Congress include these counts and how they were counted.

elements.title: Agency leaders and Congress are fully and currently informed
elements.description: The head of the agency and Congress learn about serious problems and deficiencies promptly, with what’s being done to correct them, and the public can read the office’s reports.

measures.title: Semiannual reports on time
measures.description: Whether each semiannual report reaches the agency head by April 30 and October 31, for the six months ending March 31 and September 30.

measures.title: Reports posted within 3 days
measures.description: The share of final audit, inspection, and evaluation reports posted on the office’s website within 3 days of being submitted in final form.

elements.title: Problems that are found get corrected
elements.description: Recommendations get a management decision, and agreed corrective actions are carried out and tracked until they’re complete.

measures.title: Open recommendations
measures.description: Significant recommendations from earlier reports whose corrective action isn’t complete yet, with how long they’ve been open and any potential cost savings. Semiannual reports to Congress list them.

measures.title: Reports awaiting a management decision
measures.description: Reports from earlier periods with no management decision yet, with the reasons and a target date for one. Semiannual reports to Congress list them.

elements.title: People can raise concerns safely
elements.description: Employees and the public can report possible wrongdoing through clear channels, with their identities kept confidential and protection from reprisal.

measures.title: Time to review and route a matter
measures.description: How long it takes from when a complaint, allegation, or disclosure arrives until it’s reviewed and routed. The office sets its own target.

measures.title: Whistleblower retaliation found
measures.description: Cases of whistleblower retaliation the office establishes, with the consequences imposed. Semiannual reports to Congress include them.

elements.title: Complaint, Allegation & Disclosure Intake
elements.description: Ability to receive, acknowledge, classify, and appropriately route allegations of wrongdoing, fraud, waste, abuse, and relevant disclosures through authorized channels.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Confidentiality and routing rules vary. Specific retaliation complaints or protected disclosures may need referral to another legally authorized entity.

elements.title: Audit, Inspection & Evaluation
elements.description: Ability to plan, conduct, supervise, or coordinate independent, objective examinations of programs, operations, performance, and controls.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Methodologies, mandatory reviews, professional standards, and jurisdiction depend on the OIG and engagement.

elements.title: Investigation Management
elements.description: Ability to assess allegations within jurisdiction, plan authorized investigative work, manage evidence and case progress, and document investigative results or referrals.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Law enforcement powers, case types, investigative jurisdiction, evidence handling, and disclosure restrictions vary by legal authority.

elements.title: Recommendations & Corrective Action Monitoring
elements.description: Ability to issue findings or recommendations where authorized, track responses and progress, and monitor implementation of corrective measures.
elements.applicabilityNotes: OIGs generally recommend and monitor; they do not universally possess authority to implement or compel agency corrective actions.

elements.title: Oversight Reporting & Communication
elements.description: Ability to communicate independent oversight findings, recommendations, material risks, and work results to the appropriate officials and public audiences consistent with law.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Reporting cadence, content, recipients, and confidentiality depend on legal requirements and the sensitivity of the work. Whistleblower education and coordination may be separate supporting functions.

elements.title: Review and route each matter
elements.description: Review each matter for jurisdiction and priority, and route it to the right team or to another authority, recording the decision and the reason.

elements.title: Protect the identity of people who report
elements.description: Limit who can see the identity of a person who reports to the people who need it, consistent with applicable law.

elements.title: Keep evidence linked to its case
elements.description: Link evidence and records to the case they belong to, with a record of who handled them and when.

elements.title: Restrict access to case information
elements.description: Limit access to case information to the people assigned to the case or otherwise authorized, and keep a record of access.

elements.title: Plan oversight work
elements.description: Keep a plan of audits, inspections, and evaluations, with each one’s scope, schedule, and status.

elements.title: Document work and findings
elements.description: Keep the work papers and evidence behind each finding, so a reviewer can trace how it was reached.

elements.title: Keep a quality program, with external peer reviews
elements.description: Check the quality of audits, inspections, and evaluations against the standards they follow, and for audits under the Yellow Book, have an external peer review at least once every 3 years.

elements.title: Track each recommendation until it’s closed
elements.description: Record each recommendation with its owner, the response, target dates, and status, until it’s closed.

elements.title: Report on open recommendations
elements.description: Produce a current list of open recommendations and their status whenever it’s needed.

elements.title: Compile periodic reports
elements.description: Gather the results of the period’s work for periodic reports to agency leadership and Congress.

elements.title: Publish reports
elements.description: Publish reports and summaries to the public where appropriate, in accessible formats.

elements.title: Oversight Case Management
elements.description: An example architecture: one case system for the office’s oversight and investigative work, administered by the office, that carries each matter from intake through triage, referral, investigation, and closure, with access limited by assignment and the statistics oversight reporting needs.

parts: Intake forms for the hotline and for staff, feeding one intake queue
Triage with recorded decisions, and referrals to other authorities
Case records with assignment, status, and investigative steps
Evidence records with chain of custody
Access limited by case assignment, with the identities of people who report restricted further
Statistics for the semiannual report
strengths: Each matter is one record, from intake to closure
The office controls who administers it and who sees what
Statistics for oversight reporting come from the records themselves
fitsWhen: The office runs investigations with evidence and referrals for prosecution
Independence from the agency’s own systems matters
watchFor: Early configuration choices, such as case types, are hard to change later
Data from older systems needs moving and cleaning up
A hosted system needs a security authorization before it can hold case information

ways.title: An oversight case product
ways.description: A case management product made for oversight and investigative work, configured for the office and administered by it.
strengths: Built around investigative work, such as evidence handling and referrals
Comes with reports shaped for oversight reporting
fitsWhen: There’s budget for licenses and an administrator in the office
watchFor: Another product to buy, secure, and keep up

ways.title: The agency’s shared case platform
ways.description: The office’s own case types on the agency’s shared case platform, with administration and access the office controls.
strengths: Uses licenses, skills, and security approvals the agency already has
fitsWhen: The agency runs a case platform, and the office can control who administers its part
watchFor: The office’s independence depends on keeping its administration and access apart from the agency’s
Evidence handling, such as chain of custody, usually needs building

elements.title: Confidential Online Hotline
elements.description: An example architecture: a public web form and phone line for reporting fraud, waste, and abuse that can take anonymous reports, keeps the identity of the person reporting apart from the allegation, and gives them a code to check back or add information.

parts: A public web form linked directly from the office’s home page, and a phone line
A choice to report anonymously, or to ask that one’s identity be kept confidential
Contact details stored apart from the allegation, visible only to the people who need them
A report code the person can use to check back or add information without identifying themselves
Delivery of each report into the intake queue
strengths: Makes reporting easy, through the direct link the law asks for
Protects identities by design rather than by habit
Lets the office follow up with people who report anonymously
fitsWhen: The office receives reports from the public or from employees
The office’s current form sends reports to a shared inbox
watchFor: Anonymous reports are hard to act on without a way to follow up
Spam and duplicate reports need screening before triage
What people type must not be recorded anywhere outside the intake system, such as in web analytics

elements.title: Audit Management & Work Papers
elements.description: An example architecture: one place for the office’s plan of audits, inspections, and evaluations, the work papers and evidence behind each finding, supervisors’ review sign-offs, and the recommendations each report makes.

parts: A plan of oversight work with each engagement’s scope, schedule, and status
Electronic work papers with evidence attached, cross-referenced to the report
Supervisors’ review notes and sign-offs, kept with the work papers
Findings and recommendations recorded once, then tracked to closure
Records retention for closed engagements
strengths: Supports the documentation and supervision that professional standards require
Peer reviewers can trace each finding to its evidence
Recommendations start in the same place they’re tracked
fitsWhen: The office follows the Yellow Book or the Blue Book for its audits, inspections, and evaluations
Work papers live in shared drives today
watchFor: Teams need time to adopt a new way of documenting their work
Evidence with sensitive personal information needs the same protection it has elsewhere
Older engagements usually stay where they are, so there are two places to look for a while

ways.title: An audit management product
ways.description: A product made for audit work, with electronic work papers, review sign-offs, and recommendations built in.
strengths: The documentation and supervision steps come built in
Reporting across engagements, such as on open recommendations, is part of it
fitsWhen: The office has many engagements at a time
watchFor: Another product to buy, secure, and keep up

ways.title: Work papers in the collaboration workspace
ways.description: A workspace for each engagement in the agency’s collaboration suite, with work paper templates, and supervisors’ sign-offs recorded through document approvals.
strengths: Uses tools the office already has and knows
Costs little to start, and is easy to change
fitsWhen: The office is small, with a few engagements at a time
watchFor: Cross-references and review sign-offs depend on discipline, which peer reviews will test
Reporting across engagements, such as on open recommendations, takes manual work

elements.title: Shared Recommendation Tracker
elements.description: An example architecture: a recommendation tracker the office owns, where agency officials submit corrective action plans, updates, and evidence through their own access, and the office decides when each recommendation is closed.

parts: One record per recommendation, with its report, owner, agreed action, target date, and status
Agency access limited to their own recommendations, for submitting plans, updates, and evidence
The office’s review of each submission, with the decision to close recorded
Reminders before target dates
Lists of open recommendations for the semiannual report, the website, and the agency’s budget justification
strengths: Replaces email and spreadsheets traded back and forth with the agency
The office keeps the decision to close, and the agency keeps responsibility for acting
The same data serves the semiannual report and the agency’s GAO-IG Act report
fitsWhen: The office has many open recommendations across several parts of the agency
Status is gathered by email before each semiannual report
watchFor: Agency users need accounts and guidance, which takes coordination
Giving agency officials access must not expose anything else the office holds
What it takes to close a recommendation needs agreeing with the agency up front

ways.title: A module of the audit product
ways.description: The audit product’s recommendation module, opened to agency officials for their own recommendations.
fitsWhen: The office’s audit product has a module like this
watchFor: Agency officials need access to the office’s product, limited to their own recommendations

ways.title: An app the office owns on a platform
ways.description: A tracker the office builds and administers on a platform, kept apart from the agency’s other apps.
fitsWhen: The office’s audit tools have no module agency officials can use
watchFor: The office keeps the app working, and in step with its audit tools

elements.title: Oversight Reporting from Source Data
elements.description: An example architecture: a reporting store fed by the case, audit, and recommendation systems that produces the semiannual report’s statistics, with a publishing step that posts final reports to the office’s website and Oversight.gov within 3 days.

parts: Feeds from the case, audit, and recommendation systems into one reporting store
A definition of each statistic the semiannual report needs, kept with the data
Draft tables for each reporting period, for review
A publishing step that posts final reports to the website and Oversight.gov, recording the date
strengths: Statistics are counted the same way every period
Less gathering by hand before each deadline
The date each report was posted is on record
fitsWhen: Each semiannual report takes weeks of gathering by hand
Counts get questioned because they’re compiled differently each time
watchFor: It’s only as good as the data in the systems that feed it
Each definition needs an owner for when the law or guidance changes
Sensitive details must stay out of anything published

ways.title: A reporting store fed by the office’s systems

elements.title: Data Analytics for Oversight Planning
elements.description: An example architecture: the office’s data team brings agency financial, payment, and program data into an analytics workspace, where rules and models point to risks, such as unusual payments or duplicate vendors, that help plan audits and open investigations.

parts: Agreements and regular feeds for the agency data the office has a right to, such as payments, contracts, and grants
Rules and models that flag risks, each with the reason it was flagged
A review step where auditors or investigators decide what to look into
A record of what was flagged, what was decided, and what came of it
Controls that keep each use of the data within the office’s authority
strengths: Points audits and investigations at the highest risks
Finds patterns across large data sets that sampling misses
Results show which risk indicators are worth keeping
fitsWhen: The office has, or can get, regular access to agency data
It has staff who can build and check analytics, or can hire them
watchFor: A flag isn’t a finding, so every lead needs review and evidence before anything is done
Models can carry gaps or bias in the data, so their results need checking over time
Data sharing agreements and privacy rules limit what can be combined

elements.title: Audit Work Papers in the Collaboration Workspace
elements.description: An example architecture: each engagement gets a workspace in the agency’s collaboration suite, with folders and templates for work papers, cross-references to the report, and supervisors’ review recorded through document approvals.

parts: A workspace for each engagement, made from a template with standard folders
Work paper templates with fields for purpose, source, conclusion, and cross-references
Supervisors’ review and sign-off through document approvals, with dates
A shared list that tracks each engagement’s plan, status, and recommendations
Retention labels for closed engagements, with access limited to the team
strengths: Uses tools the office already has and knows
Costs little to start, and is easy to change
fitsWhen: The office is small, with a few engagements at a time
It isn’t ready to buy and set up an audit product
watchFor: Cross-references and review sign-offs depend on discipline, which peer reviews will test
Reporting across engagements, such as on open recommendations, takes manual work
Collaboration tools make sharing easy, so access to engagement workspaces needs limiting

elements.title: Digital Evidence Store
elements.description: An example architecture: secure storage for investigations’ digital evidence, such as forensic images, video, and large email collections, with each item linked to its case and a record of everyone who handled it.

parts: Storage for large files, such as forensic images and video, kept apart from everyday systems
Each item linked to its case, with where and when it was collected
A custody log of every access, copy, and transfer
Hashes that show an item hasn’t changed since it was collected
Retention and disposal by the case’s records schedule, with holds during litigation
strengths: Shows that evidence hasn’t been altered
Handles files too large for the case system
Evidence can go to prosecutors as a controlled copy
fitsWhen: The office collects digital evidence, such as devices or email
Evidence sits on drives or in shared folders today
watchFor: Storage costs grow with forensic images and video
Access needs to be as tightly limited as the cases themselves
Sharing with prosecutors and courts needs a defined process

ways.title: A digital evidence management product
ways.description: A product made for managing digital evidence, with custody logs and hashing built in.
fitsWhen: The office handles large amounts of digital evidence
watchFor: Another product to buy, secure, and keep up

ways.title: Secure storage with a custody log
ways.description: Encrypted storage in the agency’s cloud or data center, kept apart for the office, with a custody log the office builds and links to its case system.
fitsWhen: The office handles digital evidence now and then
watchFor: The custody log and hashing carry the evidence’s weight, so they must be built and checked with care

relations.description: Takes reports from the public, including anonymous ones. Classifying and routing them happens in the case system it feeds.
Suggests a category and where to route each allegation, and intake staff decide. What the model sees must keep the identity of people who report confidential.
Helps choose and scope audits, inspections, and evaluations. Doing and documenting them happens elsewhere.
Finds leads. Each one is assessed and investigated in the case system.
Keeps digital evidence and its custody. The case itself is managed in the case system.
Lists of open recommendations for the semiannual report and the website. The rest of the report comes from elsewhere.
Drafts of routine notices and report sections, with the office’s wording, from the case and audit data.
The office’s case types and steps are the shared platform, set up for oversight.
Each item of digital evidence is linked to its case.
Each report lands in the product’s intake queue.
Each report lands in the office’s intake queue on the platform, kept apart from other offices.
The workspaces, approvals, and retention labels are the agency’s collaboration suite.
Recommendations start in the audit reports and are tracked to closure here.
Case statistics for the semiannual report.
Risks it finds feed the plan of oversight work.
